claims.text: The baseline material is an as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi thin film.
FeMnNiGeSi thin films can be fabricated by conventional room-temperature sputtering.
The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi films possess inherent residual stresses.
The homogeneous FeMnNiGeSi films have limited thermal dissipation.
The controlled intervention is to alternate approximately 20 nm FeMnNiGeSi layers with approximately 5 nm conductive-metal interlayers.
Cu is suitable as a high-thermal-conductivity interlayer.
Conductive interlayers create interfaces that promote faster and more spatially uniform heat dissipation.
Faster interlayer heat transfer moderates local thermal gradients during magnetic-cooling cycles.
Local thermal gradients produce localized overheating during rapid magnetic-cooling cycles.
Localized overheating promotes thermally induced stress concentrations.
Thermally induced stress concentrations and hotspots promote domain-wall pinning.
Reducing thermal gradients will reduce domain-wall pinning and make the magnetocaloric response more reversible.
Conductive interlayers decouple the heat-transfer bottleneck from intrinsic magnetic-domain dynamics.
The multilayer will exhibit a sharper magnetocaloric entropy-change curve than the homogeneous film.
The multilayer magnetocaloric response will be more reproducible than that of the homogeneous film.
The multilayer will exhibit reduced magnetic hysteresis, especially at higher cycling frequencies.
Adding the interlayers may shift the onset temperature of the magnetocaloric effect.
The proposed effect applies below 100 Oe, around the magnetic transition, and when cycling approaches the thermal-dissipation limit of the homogeneous film.
A representative operating-temperature boundary for the proposed effect is 150–350 K.
Conductive interlayers may adversely affect magnetic coupling across the multilayer.
